en: The lay practitioner Jinghui has completed the carving of the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Guān jīng). Some have raised an objection, stating that Chan is not a matter of conceptual thought, whereas this sūtra relies entirely on visualization to attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Since the lay practitioner already stands within the lineage of the Patriarchs, he ought to exert himself in upholding the ancestral Way; now...
"Is this not causing people to become mired in mere bypaths? I maintain that these are but shallow views regarding the vulgar discourse on the Pure Land;

they do not understand the ultimate aim of true Zen. Now, when one penetrates to the utmost clarity and realizes the mind and its nature, one must inevitably fix the mindfulness upon a single point, not allowing it to leak away into the realm of profit and desire, where it would collide with the five turbidities. After a long time..."
When the sphere of mental activity ceases and both feeling and perception are empty, phenomena do not persist and the Buddha does not stand; only then is Great Liberation fully realized.
How could it be merely the Tathāgata-Buddha? This is truly a dried piece of excrement—it is the Zen of the Patriarchs, which is called "the bowl falling over the cliff.

Lately, those who attain awakening through the supernatural powers of latent consciousness are everywhere; yet, how few are willing to scour away perverse thoughts within stillness and silence to refine themselves into [true realization].

Perfect Enlightenment. Although one does not wait for the sixteen contemplations or for the mirror-image to appear before the eyes, by seeing the Buddha within the nine grades of lotus-wombs, it is certain that one has already undergone a thorough transformation.

Daily life will naturally become pure, and the *Sambhogakāya* (Peaceful Radiance) will spontaneously manifest before you—far superior to merely studying words and phrases in books, thereby committing the karma of slandering the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Layman, observe this present Chan...
Alas! It is a painful injury that the ancestral Way has declined, such that all people now rush outward in pursuit of things, engaging in the evil habit of seizing and plundering.
I have specifically extracted this sutra to serve as a corrective for them, so that each may reflect inwardly upon it.
This is truly an urgent aid for restoring social customs and transforming the world; how could it be subject to debate?
In the autumn of the Yiwu year of the Shunzhi era, the Elder of Nanhu, Xingsheng Baoweng, composed this preface:
Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition. What is this "great matter"? It is birth-and-death.
This is a matter of great importance. Thus, it begins with the preaching of the Dharma and concludes with the holding up of a flower;

it is nothing more than the desire for all sentient beings to individually realize Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Yet, while there are no two paths back to the source, there are many gates of expedient means.
If one seeks the swiftest path to bring an end to birth and death, nothing surpasses Chan meditation for realizing the Way. And among the most swift of these swift paths, the direct route—
Among the direct paths, there is none more supreme as a skillful means than the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Yet, among those of intelligence and talent in this world, many often disparage it as the practice of fools and women.

Indeed, to recite the name of Amitābha with the mouth while harboring defilements in the mind, or to aspire for the Peaceful Nurturing Land (An-yang) while the thoughts remain bound to this Sahā world—this is truly contemptible.
As for those who are truly able to practice the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo), their profound stillness penetrates the subtle, and they enter the wondrous through silent contemplation;
subject and object are both forgotten, and phenomena and principle are unified.

To disparage such practitioners is, as the Zen Master Tianru truly said, not to disparage the common man or woman, but rather to disparage Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, as well as Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna. This is what the Buddha taught.
The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* must not fail to be recited.

Although this sūtra contains the complete sixteen methods of visualization, the visualization of the Buddha is especially the essential core of the entire work. One who visualizes skillfully perceives all appearances as being without appearance.
One can then perceive the entire body of Amitābha; by viewing all phenomena as illusory, one can enter the true realm of the Pure Land;
and by contemplating the selflessness of one's own body, one can possess the right view of the Tathāgata.
Thus, from a single Tathāgata, one perceives infinite Tathāgatas; entering a single realm, one pervades infinite pure lands. Awakening...
The single Dharma-body merges with infinite Dharma-bodies. It is mindfulness without thought, cultivation without practice, and realization without attainment.
Is this not the mark of one who has thoroughly understood the great causal conditions? Master Wujin of Tiantai was a "tiger of meaning" within the teachings;

he was profoundly versed in the Three Contemplations. His diagrams were exquisite and his verses concise yet elegant. Alas, as time passed, these works became obscured and overgrown; it is to be hoped they may now be propagated.
It is extremely rare; therefore, I have specially commissioned this edition for circulation.

Furthermore, I have provided a brief commentary on one or two historical precedents to assist beginners, so that those who see or hear it may fix their eyes upon the images and be moved in heart by the text, thereby rejoicing and praising with admiration, generating the unsurpassed resolve, and together forming a superior affinity for the Pure Land.
Even those who harbor doubts or slander will plant no small amount of wholesome causes.
It is like the old woman east of the city who vowed never to see the Buddha; though she covered her face with her hands, she could ultimately not escape him.

How much more so for those whose consciousness has once passed through the field of awareness, which forever becomes the seed of the Way? Know that this matter does not depend on whether one is close or distant, nor does it distinguish between the sharp or dull faculties;

each possesses their own inherent Amitābha, which spontaneously manifests as the Pure Land of Mind-Only. Therefore, even those who have committed the ten evils and the five heinous crimes [are not excluded].
Moreover, even those who attain rebirth through ten recitations, or who maintain the name with a distracted mind, may likewise ascend to the Land of Bliss.

Yet those who harbor doubt and slander are like caged birds or fish in a cauldron; they mistakenly call their confinement happiness and falsely reckon the fleeting as enduring—like a horse in a crack or a bubble on water.

One can only fear that once one’s physical strength fails and the spirit becomes confused, neither the power of one's writings nor the "god of wealth" will be able to pull one back, as the path ahead remains shrouded in mist.
Vast and boundless; there is no fundamental basis upon which to rely. This causes those of intelligence and talent to be ridiculed, instead, by the ignorant and simple-minded.
I venture to request that you directly accept this and enter together into the ocean of Amitābha’s vows.
Written on an autumn day in the year of Yiwei (1895), by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Zhang Wenjia, styled Zhongjiafu,
after bathing and purifying himself,
in homage to the *Buddhabhāṣita-Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* (with appended illustrations and verses).
Translated by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
Thus have I heard... [up to] Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, acting as the leader.
Compiled from the Sūtra with Verses; narrated by the Tiantai Master Wujin (Wu-yin), the Lamp-Transmitter.
At this auspicious assembly on Vulture Peak,
the Tathāgata sits cross-legged; surrounded by the multitudes of the Three Vehicles and the eight classes of beings,
he is tranquil yet ever-illuminating, discerning the capacities and needs of all like a great bell awaiting a strike.
Having long cultivated and long realized the true samādhi, when mind and object are as they are (*tathatā*) and pure, only then can one attain rebirth in non-retrogression.
For those of perfect capacity, you should preach according to their nature;
at that time, from the great city of Rājagṛha... [down to] ...one shall not go.
King Ajātaśatru imprisoned his father;
he was named Ajātaśatru because from birth he was accompanied by the signs of enmity and malice.
Following the instructions of his evil friend Devadatta, you murdered Bimbisāra to become the new king.
I have murdered the Muni to become a new Buddha; it is truly a joy to transform the world together with him.
Following the teachings, King You (幽王) strictly restricted his inner chambers, forbidding all his ministers from entering.
According to the Sanskrit *Ajātaśatru*, this means "One Whose Enemy Was Not Yet Born. While his mother was pregnant with him, there were signs of resentment and malice.
A diviner predicted this in advance; thus, he was named accordingly. ○ Devadatta was the Buddha’s younger cousin, also known as Ti-p'o-da-duo (Devadatta).
He had been an enemy of the Buddha throughout successive lifetimes. By means of various transformations and illusions, he sought to sway the prince's mind.
Having established a great vihāra and received extensive offerings, he said to the prince: "I shall kill the Muni and become a new Buddha; you shall kill [the current one]."
"Bimbisāra, having become a new king, you shall transform the world together with me; would that not be most delightful?
He then instructed the prince to release five hundred intoxicated elephants to trample and kill the Tathāgata. The Buddha entered the samādhi of loving-kindness and extended his hand to show them.

Immediately from his five fingers, five lions emerged. Upon seeing them, the elephants were struck with terror, threw themselves to the ground, and paid him homage. The Buddha said to the assembly: "I, at..."
At that time, there were actually no lions on the tips of his five fingers; rather, it was through the power of his roots of goodness in compassion that they were subdued.
Later, he again smeared lethal poison on the claws of his fingers, intending to wound the Buddha while prostrating himself.
Before he had even reached him, the earth spontaneously split open, and a flaming chariot came to meet him; he entered hell alive.
The State Grand Lady (up to: her countenance was serene and joyful.
The Lady [Mahāprajāpatī] went secretly to the State Grand Lady Vaidehī; when [the King] respectfully attended the Great King, she went secretly.
His body was smeared with parched-rice flour and honey, and a garland of fresh juice was placed upon him; day by day he offered these as food for the Great King.
Having eaten, he rinsed his mouth and paid homage toward the Buddha. The Venerable One conferred the precepts and preached the Dharma to him;
for twenty-one days his countenance remained harmonious and joyful, and being serene and pure, he attained the state of immortality.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru— having prevented [his father] from emerging again and having committed the evil deed of murdering his mother—
came to question the gatekeeper: "Does my father king still exist?"
The gatekeeper reported the matter in full as above. Ajātaśatru, filled with rage, intended to assassinate his mother, Candraprabhā, and the two ministers, Jīvaka and [the other].
Pressing his sword against them, he admonished them sternly until their anger finally subsided;
he then commanded the inner officials to place them under strict confinement, confining them within the deep palace and forbidding them from leaving.
At that time, Vaidehī—[having reached the point of asking] how she might behold Amitābha Buddha and the Land of Ultimate Bliss—[the narrative begins with] the causal origin of the regicide;
Vaidehī’s piteous plea gave rise to the inception of this sutra.
[This account of] the regicide causes people to develop a profound weariness for the suffering of Saṃsāra.
Even toward one's own biological children it is thus; how could others not rise up with drawn swords?
With the lotus flowers of Sukhāvatī as both mother and father, there is neither enemy nor kin—the Dharma is equal.
How great is the power of skillful means! It causes all living beings everywhere to attain peaceful nourishment.
Vaidhī, from afar, entreated toward Gṛdhrakūṭa: "O Tathāgata, when you have vanished from the mountain, appear within my palace!
What sins did I commit in the past to give birth to such a son? I only pray that I may be reborn in the realm free from sorrow.
Immediately, he emitted light, revealing all the lands; The world of Sukhāvatī appeared before her very eyes.
The three kinds of meritorious karma are the prerequisites; the sixteen gates of contemplation follow as the explanation.
The Buddha addressed Vaidehī... [up to] ...this is called the first contemplation.
Regarding "the setting sun":
when first beginning, one should observe the setting sun; its form is like a suspended drum.
Bind the mind to it and restrain the mind at a single point to accomplish great matters—how much more so when facing west to show the direction of birth.
After a long time, the mind becomes tranquil and does not waver; when stillness reaches its peak, clarity arises and contemplation is easily accomplished.
Whether with eyes open or closed, one is always clearly aware; this is the primary gateway to the Pure Land.
Next, one should practice the visualization of water (up to the point where it is called) the second visualization.
The great waters freeze into ice;
the ground of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is of lapis lazuli treasure. When one first attempts to observe it, it is not easily accomplished;
the freezing of the great waters into ice roughly resembles it, yet the realm of lapis lazuli has already appeared before one.
Below, there is a jeweled banner that supports [the structure], with eight facets on each of the eight directions, all perfectly complete.
Each side is composed of a hundred jewels; its various adornments are difficult to describe in full.
Regarding the "eight winds": in the four intermediate directions and the eight cardinal points, there are eight kinds of winds that bring about natural bliss and manifest wondrous [sounds].

The Sound of the Dharma: There are eight sufferings in the world, namely: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates being in full force.
The Buddha said to the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya: "Do you know whether form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent or impermanent?"
"Is it suffering? Is it not suffering? Is it empty? Is it not empty? Is there a self? Is there no self?
When the five bhikṣus heard this, their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated; they became arhats.
When this visualization is accomplished (up to the point where it is called) "false contemplation," when the visualization of the lapis lazuli jewel ground and water is accomplished,
the ground has already been formed. Contemplate each one individually until they are clearly manifest.
Whether with eyes closed or open, there is no loss of mindfulness; except at the time of eating, one constantly recollects this matter.
This is called the coarse vision of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. If one attains samādhi, it is inconceivable:
eighty billion kalpas of heavy offenses will be eliminated. One who performs this contemplation is said to have right contemplation.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: [This concludes] up to what is called the Fourth Meditation.
There are seven tiers of rows of trees;
each row of trees is eight thousand *yojanas* in height, and their flowers and leaves are made of the seven treasures and display various colors.
A net of exquisite pearls completely covers it above; seven rows of trees stand together with various nets.
Celestial youths dwell within palaces of wondrous flowers, adorned by the light of myriad jewels like hundreds of thousands of suns.
Exquisite flowers spring forth bearing wonderful fruits, their shapes resembling the vases of Śakra.
According to the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra], furthermore, in that land, trees made of the seven treasures fill the world:
gold trees, silver trees, lapis lazuli trees, crystal trees, coral trees, agate trees, and musaragalva trees.
The Sanskrit term *śakrābhilagna* is translated here as "the Victorious" (*nengsheng*). The Sanskrit term *maṇi* is translated as "free from defilement" (*li gou*). It says:
This jewel-light is pure and is not defiled by impurities; furthermore, it increases [in power], meaning that wherever this jewel is located, its majestic virtue increases.
Alternatively, it may be translated as "according to one's wish" or "as desired. Jāmbūnada gold is here called "supreme gold."
"Jambū" is the Sanskrit term *Jambūnada*. It refers to a tree located in the western region to the southwest of Mount Sumeru.
This tree is tall and large in form, and its fruit is sweet and delicious. When the juice of this fruit enters the water, the sand and stones turn into gold.
If a single grain [of that gold] is placed among ordinary gold, the latter all lose their luster. The Buddha’s body is like it; it is like the vase of Śakra. Śakra...
In the Sanskrit language, Śakrendra means "Capable Lord" (Nengzhu), signifying that he is able to serve as the Lord of Heaven. Regarding the term "vase" (ping):
formerly there was a poor man who constantly made offerings to a deity for twelve full years, seeking wealth and status.
Moved by compassion for this man, the deity personally gave him a vessel named the "Vase of Virtue" (De-ping) and spoke to him, saying: "Whatever things you require, from [this vase]..."
When this vase appears, that person shall obtain whatever they desire and lack nothing.
Now, because these various fruits emerge from the exquisite flowers just as that celestial vase produces all manner of objects, it is used as a metaphor for it.
Next, one should visualize water; this is called the fifth visualization.
The water of eight virtues in the eight ponds of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is each composed of the seven treasures.
From that king of soft and supple jewels, a fountain gushes forth divided into fourteen branches;
its channels are of gold, its sands are diamond-dust, and sixty billion lotuses of the seven treasures bloom there.
Water flows through the trees above and below, while birds that preach the Dharma and transform beings extol the Triple Gem.
According to the eight meritorious qualities of water: first, it is limpid and pure; second, it is cool and refreshing; third, it is sweet and delicious; fourth, it is light and soft;

fifth, it is moistening and lustrous; sixth, it is peaceful and harmonious; seventh, it removes hunger and thirst; eighth, it nourishes and develops the sense faculties. Possessing these eight kinds of merit, it benefits all sentient beings.
The land of various jewels (up to) is called "erroneous contemplation.
Contemplating the total environment and its support—
the lapis lazuli ground with eight intersecting roads— each boundary is marked by golden cords.
Above the realms are five hundred billion jeweled towers, within which the devas perform music;
furthermore, musical instruments are suspended in the void, sounding spontaneously without being struck.
By recollecting the Triple Gem, when this visualization is perfected, it is called "coarse vision" of the jeweled trees, jeweled grounds, and jeweled ponds.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the two Bodhisattvas.
As the Buddha remained in mid-air,
just as the Tathāgata was about to preach the *Buddhānusmṛti*, the Three Holy Ones of the Western Quarter suddenly appeared before him.
The body of Amitābha is like Jambu-river gold; His marks and signs and radiant light are beyond compare.
Avalokiteśvara attends to his left, Mahāsthāmaprāpta to his right; He causes the great assembly of Vaidehī to see them all.
I have now, by means of the Buddha, beheld them; But how shall future sentient beings behold them?
The Buddha told Vaidehī (up to): "This is called a false contemplation.
Regarding the precious lotus throne:
the verse states that the lotus has eighty-four thousand petals, and the number of veins and rays is exactly equal to that.
Each leaf measures twelve thousand li across; five hundred billion pearls serve as its radiant adornments.
Each *ni* pearl emits a thousand rays of light, and these rays are like canopies made of the seven treasures, with pedestals fashioned from *vaidūrya* gems.
Two kinds of precious jewel nets provide further ornamentation.
Upon the platform there naturally appears a jeweled banner, its four pillars like Mount Sumeru;
the jeweled canopy atop the banner is like a celestial palace, adorned with five hundred billion pearls.
These pearls emit eighty-four thousand rays of light, each ray manifesting in various distinct colors.
Clouds of *vajra*-pearl *saṃpuṣpita* flowers perform the Buddha-works according to the twelve [aspirations].
According to the traditions of the Western Regions, there is the *candana* tree (Jintushujia), which possesses the colors of the seven jewels and is as vast in form as Mount Sumeru;
because the color of this jewel resembles these [flowers], it is named accordingly. As for Mount Sumeru, it is called "Wondrous High" (*Miaogao*) above; it is like the Yāma [heaven].
"Deva" (天) here means "Auspicious Time" (善時). Because those beings perceive light without the distinction between day and night, it is called "Auspicious Time.
As for Amitābha Buddha, in his past causal stage, he was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Dharmākara.
In the presence of the World-Dharma King Buddha, he made forty-eight vows to take up this pure land and gather all wholesome thoughts;
now that the power of those vows has been fulfilled, it causes his support—the lotus throne—to be such as this.
The Buddha told Ānanda: [up to] "Samyaksaṃbuddha. Next, one should visualize that the Buddha’s lotus throne has been completed;
one should then visualize the Buddha. How can sentient beings come to see him?
The Dharma-realm body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas Constantly enters the worlds of practitioners.
Therefore, you should contemplate the Buddha with your mind; This mind is itself the marks and signs and radiant light.
This mind creates the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha; The three titles are all produced from the contemplation of the mind.
Regarding the visualization of that Buddha (up to) attaining the *nien-fo* samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*):
first perform the visualization of the image;
before visualizing the true Buddha, first imagine the Buddha’s body as being like Jambūnada gold.
Seated upon that flower, the mind’s eye opens; the adornments of Sukhāvatī are most clearly perceived.
To the left sits Avalokiteśvara, and to the right, Mahāsthāmaprāpta; all three figures radiate great beams of light.
Beneath each tree are three lotus flowers, and the Three Holy Ones constantly together proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
Regarding "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (正徧知): it is one of the ten epithets of a Tathāgata. Because it is immeasurably profound, it is metaphorically compared to the ocean.
In Sanskrit, *Tathāgata* means "Thus-Come One" (如來); in Sanskrit, *Arhat* means "Worthy of Offerings" (應供);
in Sanskrit, *Samyaksaṃbuddha* means "Perfectly and Fully Awakened One" (正徧知). These are all general designations for all Buddhas.
Title. The mind moves the Buddhas; the mind is itself the Buddhas. If the mind can even become all Buddhas, how could it not move Amitābha?
If the mind is already the Buddhas, how could it not be Amitābha himself?
One should know that Amitābha and all Buddhas are neither more nor less than one another. All Buddhas are the multiplicity within the unity, while Amitābha is the unity within the multiplicity.
This is the first [point]. The teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures are collectively termed *sūtra* and are all equally called "sūtras.
The Buddha told Ānanda... [up to] ...this is called false contemplation.
The Buddha’s True Dharma-body: Two verses.
The Buddha’s body is sixty million *koṭis*, hundred thousand *nayutas*, and as many *yojanas* as there are sands in the Ganges.
Its color is like that of ten million *koṭis* of Yāma heavens, and like the purple-polished gold of the Jambūnada tree.
The white curl of hair winds like five Mount Sumerus; The deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.

From every pore of his body he radiates light, Like the supreme, perfect halo of Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains, Pervading ten billion great thousandfold world systems; The emanated Buddhas are beyond measure, most numerous.

The body is endowed with eighty-four thousand marks; Each mark is endowed with eighty-four thousand secondary characteristics, And each secondary characteristic is endowed with eighty-four thousand rays of light.
These rays universally gather in those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
To see this is to see all Buddhas, And the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha is said to have been attained.
Accordingly, regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), the Buddha perceives them all as the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

Because his wisdom and principle are in profound union, he is able to manifest the physical marks, the minor characteristics, and the radiance. Therefore, each section speaks of "eighty-four thousand. As for "unconditioned compassion" (*nirālambana-maitrī*):
Without the mind engaging in攀緣 (pāraṇa, mental clinging), benefits manifest spontaneously;
all of this is the natural accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness (*maitrī-kuśalamūla*). The Master of Repentance Ciyun said:

"Those who wish to practice contemplation should go to a single location, sit cross-legged facing west on a corded meditation bench, with the neck and spine aligned, neither too erect nor too hunched. They should harmonize the breath and remain settled."
With his mind, he should directly visualize the sixteen-foot golden body of Amitābha Buddha seated upon a lotus flower.
He should single-mindedly focus on the single mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows. This tuft is fifteen feet long, five inches in circumference, and has eight facets on its exterior.
The tuft is hollow within, spiraling to the right in a graceful curve; situated between the eyebrows, it is brilliantly pure, transparent, and radiantly luminous.
O Jin Yan, settle your mind and focus your thoughts; remain steadfast and do not let them waver.

Furthermore, you should observe that whatever is perceived through these mental images—whether they have been realized or not—is entirely due to the causes and conditions of thought. They possess no real nature or characteristics;

all things are empty, like the moon reflected in a mirror or its shadow, like a dream, and like an illusion. Although they are empty, they can nevertheless be seen; all of these are manifestations of the nature of the mind. Do not...
They are one and not different; neither vertical nor horizontal, they are inconceivable. When thought and mind are stilled, one can achieve the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
After a long time, one may arise from it. This is because there are eighty thousand marks (*lakṣaṇa*);

since it is difficult to perfect the visualization of them all, one is instructed to contemplate only the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which is like five Mount Sumerus. If this contemplation is perfected, all eighty thousand marks will manifest.
Furthermore, this visualization method of the fifteen-foot [Buddha] is especially suited for beginners.
The Buddha told Ānanda... [up to] ...is called wrong visualization.
The Dharmakāya of Avalokiteśvara. Verse 2.
The body of Avalokiteśvara is eighty hundred thousand nayuta yojanas in height;
his body is the color of purple-polished gold. Upon his head is a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), and the halo around his neck extends for one hundred thousand yojanas on each side.
His five hundred transformation bodies are like those of Śākyamuni.
Each Buddha has five hundred transformed attendants; within them appear the sentient beings of the five realms of existence.
A *vimala* jewel serves as their celestial crown (*tīrṇamukuṭa*).
Within the celestial crown stands a transformed Buddha, complete with the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white hair-tuft) mark and the colors of the seven jewels, emitting eighty-four thousand rays of light.
Within the light, emanated Buddhas and emanated attendants appear;
like red lotuses with immeasurable radiance, their hands and feet are adorned with all the marks and signs, each exactly as described in the sutras.
According to the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāraṇī used his supernormal powers to look upward for thirty-two Ganges-sands of worlds.

Even a sandalwood world-system could not see the crown of the Buddha’s head; therefore, it is called the "invisible-crown-mark" (anavalokitamūrdha-lakṣaṇa). It does not reach that of the World-Honored One.
Next, one contemplates the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta... [up to] Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The Dharmakāya of Śrīkṣetra: Two Verses on the Dimensions of Śrīkṣetra’s Body Being Equal to Those of Avalokiteśvara.

When the light from the entire body illuminates the lands of the ten directions, and one beholds the light from the pores of the Bodhisattva, one immediately perceives the pure and wondrous radiance of all Buddhas.
Illuminating all with the light of wisdom, he is therefore named Boundless Light (*Amitābha*).
Causing beings to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power, he is further named Great Power Attained (*Mahāsthāmaprāpta*).
Within his vast and expansive Buddha-field, there appear five hundred jeweled lotuses upon which celestial crowns rest.
The uṣṇīṣa is like a *padma* flower; within the precious vase, all manner of radiance is contained.
When he walks, the worlds tremble everywhere; when he sits, the lands shake throughout, adorned with precious flowers like the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Three Sages of the West have all gathered like clouds.
When seeing these things (up to) they constantly come to the place where this practitioner is.
One should universally observe that when seeing these things at the time of birth, one forms the perception of being born; one’s own mind is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Sitting cross-legged, visualize the lotus petals closing; Five hundred colored lights come to illuminate the body.
Behold Buddhas and Bodhisattvas filling the sky, And water birds and forest trees proclaiming the wondrous Dharma.
When emerging from concentration, it merges with concentration; Seeing thus is called "Universal Contemplation."
The Buddha told Ānanda (up to): "This is called the thirteenth contemplation.
If one wishes to give rise to a sincere mind to reach the Western Land, one should first contemplate the image of the sixteen-foot [Buddha]."
Avalokiteśvara attends on the left, Mahāsthāmaprāpta on the right;
They manifest freely throughout the ten directions, appearing sometimes sixteen feet tall, sometimes eight feet. Their manifested forms are of a true golden color;
one need only observe the head to know these two venerable ones. This is the Contemplation of Various Images of the Western Quarter.
Regarding the observation of the primary forms: he who has a transformation Buddha upon his crown is Avalokiteśvara;

Anointing the body with oil or perfuming one's robes; not going to listen to singing or dancing oneself; not eating past midday—these are the "gates" (gates of restraint) which prohibit and close off the eight transgressions so that they are not committed.

Since fasting (upavāsa) takes "not eating past midday" as its essence, and the eight matters assist in completing the essence of the fast by mutually supporting it, it is also called the "Eight-Limbed Fasting Dharma" (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa).
